pronunciation.note: The lunar dynasty of the epics — the Candravamśa — traces every lunar king to him.

domains.title: The Glittering Moon
domains.subtitle: The Lunar God, Father of the Lunar Dynasty
domains.lead: Candra is the moon personified: the glittering lord whose waxing and waning marks the calendar, whose crescent crowns Śiva’s hair, and whose dynasty — the Candravamśa — produced, by epic genealogy, the Pāṇḍavas and Krishna himself. In the Veda he is Soma’s celestial body; in later mythology he is the beautiful, cursed, forever-waning god.

cards.name: The Waxing Fortnight
cards.desc: The bright half of the month, śuklapakṣa, is his growth — the calendar’s first engine.

cards.name: Śiva’s Diadem
cards.desc: The crescent moon in Śiva’s hair is Candra’s seat — cooled by the Ganges, crowned by it.

cards.name: Father of Budha
cards.desc: By Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati, he fathered Budha — Mercury and ancestor of the lunar line.

cards.name: The Waning Curse
cards.desc: Cursed by Dakṣa to waste away for loving Tārā, he is saved by Śiva’s partial mercy — hence the phases.

mythology.lead: Candra’s mythology clusters around two stories: the theft of Tārā and its curse, and the moon-churning of the ocean of milk. He is the most beautiful of the gods and the most diminished — the waxing and waning written into his body as punishment and mercy at once.

myths.title: The Abduction of Tārā
myths.text: Candra loved Tārā, wife of the guru Bṛhaspati, and carried her off; the gods’ war over her ended with her return — and her pregnancy, which she refused to explain until the child’s radiance declared the moon his father. Budha, the child, founded the lunar dynasty through which the epic’s heroes descend.

myths.title: The Curse and the Mercy
myths.text: Dakṣa, Bṛhaspati’s champion, cursed the moon to waste to nothing; the pleading gods won a partial reprieve — the curse would lift for half each month. The phases of the moon are the scar of the love-affair, and Śiva’s wearing of the crescent is the war-god’s mercy made ornament.

myths.title: The Moon from the Churning
myths.text: When the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, the moon rose among the treasures — Dhanvantari’s medicine-chest, the apsarases, and Candra, the glittering disc. Śiva took him onto his brow; the poison of the churning, Halāhala, he drank instead, turning his throat blue.

myths.title: The Celestial Plant
myths.text: In the Veda the moon is Soma’s home: the pressed plant’s juice ascends to become the lunar disc, and the moon’s quarters are the soma-cup’s refills. The identification of moon, plant, and god is the Veda’s most compact theology — three substances, one divinity.

lore.syncretism: Candra fused with Soma in the Vedic period and with the astronomical moon (one of the nine grahas) in the medieval period. The Greeks of the Northwest compared him to Selene’s domain but found no single Olympian match; and the Buddhist lunar mansions (nakṣatras) kept his calendar alive across Asia.
lore.culturalLegacy: The lunar calendar — every Hindu festival’s dating — is his monument; the Candravamśa genealogy made him the ancestor of the epic’s heroes. The crescent in Śiva’s hair is Hinduism’s most reproduced ornament; and ‘Monday’ (somavāra) still speaks his Vedic name in every Indian week.
lore.extendedMeditation: Candra: the glittering one, restored in plain letters that glitter on the screen. His waxing and waning need no diacritic — the phases are written in the name’s rhythm, two syllables that fill and empty like the moon they name.
lore.archaeology: Candra rides the temple friezes as the lunar graha; the great crescents of the medieval Śiva temples of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are his monumental form. The astronomical observatories of Jantar Mantar measure his cycles in stone.
lore.cult: The moon’s phases govern every fast and festival — Ekādaśī, the full-moon and new-moon rites are his calendar. The soma-pressing of the Vedic ritual is his oldest liturgy, remembered in every modern pūrṇimā.
lore.iconography: A pale, beautiful god in a chariot of white horses (or the antelope’s antler-crescent), holding a lotus and a club; the crescent on Śiva’s head is his most famous seat. The twenty-seven nakṣatras — his wives, the daughters of Dakṣa — attend him.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology sets him beside Sin, Thoth, and Máni as the lunar god whose body is the calendar; and the Tārā-episode is cited in every study of the moon-god’s ‘sin’ — the waning written into myth as punishment. His name, through Monday and the lunar mansions, keeps the oldest astronomy alive in daily speech.
